title: Function: Domain and Range
notes: **Definition.** For f: A → B, the domain is A (every admissible input) and the range is { f(x) : x ∈ A }, always a subset of the codomain B. A rule without its domain does not yet define a function.

**Polynomials.** Every polynomial is defined for all real x, so f(x) = x² − 3x + 2 has domain ℝ. Completing the square gives f(x) = (x − 3/2)² − 1/4, so its least value is −1/4 and the range is [−1/4, ∞).
**Rational functions.** f(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 2) is undefined at x = 2, so Dom f = ℝ ∖ {2}. Solving y = (x + 1)/(x − 2) for x gives x = (2y + 1)/(y − 1), which needs y ≠ 1, hence Range f = ℝ ∖ {1}.
**Even roots.** √(g(x)) requires g(x) ≥ 0. For f(x) = √(9 − x²) the condition 9 − x² ≥ 0 gives −3 ≤ x ≤ 3, and the square root then runs from 0 at x = ±3 up to 3 at x = 0, so Range f = [0, 3].
**Root in a denominator.** 1/√(x² − 4) needs x² − 4 > 0, not ≥ 0, because a zero denominator is also forbidden; the domain is (−∞, −2) ∪ (2, ∞). This is the single most common domain error in exams.
**Logarithms.** ln(g(x)) requires g(x) > 0 with base positive and different from 1. So f(x) = ln(x − 1) has domain (1, ∞); since ln maps (0, ∞) onto ℝ, its range is all of ℝ.
**Composites.** For (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)), x must lie in Dom g AND g(x) must lie in Dom f. With f(x) = √x and g(x) = x − 4, the composite needs x − 4 ≥ 0, giving domain [4, ∞).

**Range by inversion.** Write y = f(x), solve for x in terms of y, then keep only those y for which the solution is real and lies in the domain. Horizontal asymptotes usually appear as the excluded y value.

**Range on a closed interval.** A continuous function on [a, b] attains its extremes; evaluate f at both endpoints and at every stationary point where f′(x) = 0, then take the smallest and largest results.
**Codomain is not the range.** f: ℝ → ℝ with f(x) = x² has codomain ℝ but range [0, ∞), so it is not onto. Shrinking the codomain to [0, ∞) makes the same rule surjective.
**One-to-one check.** f(x) = x² is not injective on ℝ because f(2) = f(−2) = 4, but on [0, ∞) it is injective and therefore invertible with inverse √x.

**Exam method.** List exclusions first (zero denominator, negative even root, non-positive log argument), intersect the resulting sets, and only then attempt the range; sketching the curve is a reliable cross-check.
summary: The domain is the set of inputs for which a real-valued formula is defined; the range is the set of values the function actually produces. Finding a domain means excluding zero denominators, negative even roots and non-positive logarithm arguments; finding a range means solving y = f(x) back for x or bounding the expression.
importantStatements: A real-valued formula defines a function only after its domain is stated.
If f is continuous on a closed interval, its range on that interval is a closed interval.
For an invertible f, the range of f equals the domain of f⁻¹.
importantNotes: A denominator that contains an even root imposes a strict inequality, not a non-strict one.
The range is a subset of the codomain; equality is exactly the surjectivity condition.
Two functions with the same formula but different domains are different functions.
examShortTricks: For (ax + b)/(cx + d), the range excludes a/c, the ratio of leading coefficients, and the domain excludes −d/c.
For √(quadratic), solve the quadratic inequality first; the range then follows from the vertex value.
To test injectivity quickly, sketch a horizontal line: more than one intersection means not one-to-one.
formulas: f: A → B;  Dom f = A;  Range f = { f(x) : x ∈ A } ⊆ B
f(x) = (ax + b)/(cx + d):  Dom f = ℝ ∖ {−d/c},  Range f = ℝ ∖ {a/c}
examples: Find the domain and range of f(x) = √(4 − x). Condition: 4 − x ≥ 0 ⇒ x ≤ 4, so Dom f = (−∞, 4]. Since √ returns non-negative values and grows without bound as x → −∞, Range f = [0, ∞).
Find the range of f(x) = 2x/(x − 3). Put y = 2x/(x − 3) ⇒ y(x − 3) = 2x ⇒ x(y − 2) = 3y ⇒ x = 3y/(y − 2), which exists only for y ≠ 2. Range f = ℝ ∖ {2}.
practiceQuestions: State the domain and range of f(x) = 1/(x² − 9).
Find the range of f(x) = √(x² + 1) and justify why it has no upper bound.
For f(x) = ln(2 − x) and g(x) = √x, determine the domain of g ∘ f.
confusion: Confusing codomain with range: f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = |x| has codomain ℝ but range [0, ∞).
Writing x² − 4 ≥ 0 for 1/√(x² − 4); equality must be excluded because the denominator would be zero.
practice: Sketch y = |x − 2| and read off its domain and range from the graph.
Build one function whose domain is ℝ ∖ {1, 2} and verify each exclusion.
universalFacts: Every polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients has range ℝ.
The image of an interval under a continuous real function is again an interval.
specialNotes: When a question says 'the function f is defined on ℝ', the domain has already been fixed for you; do not re-derive it.
Restricting the domain can make a non-injective function invertible, which is how sin x acquires arcsin x on [−π/2, π/2].
examNotes: NEB questions usually award one mark for the domain condition and one for solving the resulting inequality; show both steps.
Always state the range as a set or interval, not as an inequality alone.
importantTasks: Tabulate domain and range for six standard functions

mcs.question: The domain of f(x) = 1/√(x² − 4) is
mcs.explanation: The root requires x² − 4 ≥ 0, and the denominator excludes equality, so |x| > 2.

mcs.question: For f: ℝ → ℝ with f(x) = x², the range is
mcs.explanation: Squares of real numbers are never negative and every non-negative number is attained.
